tours.title: The Christian empire
tours.summary: From the last great persecution to the councils that defined Christian doctrine: how the religion of a minority became the religion of the Roman state in less than a century.

stops.title: The Great Persecution
stops.text: On 23 February 303, the festival of the Terminalia, soldiers demolished the new church that stood in sight of Diocletian's palace in Nicomedia. The next day an edict ordered churches destroyed, scriptures burned and Christians stripped of rank and legal rights. Further edicts ordered clergy arrested and finally all inhabitants to sacrifice. Lactantius, who taught rhetoric in Nicomedia, blamed Galerius. The persecution was severe in the East, especially in Egypt and Palestine, where Eusebius saw martyrs die, and light in the West, where Constantius hardly enforced it. It ended in 311, when the dying Galerius issued an edict of toleration asking Christians to pray for him. It was the last and largest attempt by the Roman state to eliminate Christianity.

stops.title: In this sign
stops.text: On 28 October 312 [[constantine_i|Constantine]] defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber north of Rome. Maxentius drowned when a bridge of boats collapsed under his retreating troops. Lactantius, writing soon after, says Constantine was told in a dream to mark a heavenly sign on his soldiers' shields, the chi-rho. Eusebius, many years later, reports Constantine's own account of seeing a cross of light in the sky with the words 'by this, conquer'. Two years before, a pagan panegyrist had described a vision of Apollo. Whatever happened, Constantine now credited the Christian god with his victory. The Arch of Constantine, dedicated in 315, says only that he had won 'by the inspiration of the divinity'.

stops.title: The 'Edict' of Milan
stops.text: In February 313 Constantine met his eastern colleague [[licinius|Licinius]] at Milan, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister. They agreed a policy of religious freedom for all and the return of confiscated church property. The text we have is not an edict from Milan but a letter that Licinius posted at Nicomedia in June, after defeating Maximinus Daia, preserved by Lactantius and Eusebius. It granted 'to Christians and to all others the free power to follow whatever religion each one wishes'. Constantine went much further in the following years: he gave bishops judicial powers, exempted clergy from civic duties, and built enormous churches, starting with the Lateran basilica on the site of the barracks of Maxentius' horse guard.

stops.title: Nicaea
stops.text: The empire had barely become safe for Christians when they split over the nature of Christ. An Alexandrian priest, Arius, taught that the Son was created by the Father. To settle the dispute, Constantine summoned the bishops of the empire to Nicaea in 325, about 250 to 300 of them, with travel paid by the imperial post. He opened the council himself, in purple and gold. The bishops condemned Arius and adopted a creed declaring the Son 'of one substance', homoousios, with the Father, and fixed a common rule for the date of Easter. Only two bishops refused to sign. The precedent mattered as much as the decision: an emperor convening a church council and enforcing its verdict. The quarrel went on for another sixty years.

stops.title: A new Rome on the Bosporus
stops.text: On 11 May 330 Constantine dedicated his new capital on the site of Byzantium, which he had besieged six years earlier. Constantinople had a senate, a grain dole, a hippodrome, a forum with a porphyry column topped by a statue of Constantine as the sun god, and statues looted from across the Greek world, including the serpent column from Delphi, which still stands in the hippodrome. Unlike Rome, it had no temples to the old gods built by its founder, and it had churches, including the Holy Apostles where Constantine planned to be buried among the memorials of the twelve. For more than eleven centuries it would be the capital of the Roman empire. Constantine was baptised only on his deathbed in 337, by an Arian bishop.

stops.title: The last pagan emperor
stops.text: Constantine's nephew [[julian|Julian]], raised a Christian, secretly converted to the old gods as a student of philosophy. As sole emperor from 361 he ordered temples reopened and restored, recalled exiled bishops of all parties in the hope that they would destroy each other, and forbade Christians to teach classical literature, a measure even the pagan Ammianus thought harsh. He tried to create a pagan church with a hierarchy of priests and charitable works on the Christian model, and planned to rebuild the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. His enthusiasm for sacrifices of hundreds of animals bewildered pagans as well as Christians at Antioch, where he spent the winter of 362-363. He died in Persia in June 363, and his reforms died with him.

stops.title: A governor becomes a bishop
stops.text: In 374 Milan's bishop died and the city was split between Nicene and Arian factions. The governor of the province, Ambrose, came to the church to keep order. A child's voice, the story goes, called out 'Ambrose bishop!', and the crowd took it up. He was not even baptised. Within a week he was baptised, ordained and consecrated. Ambrose became the most formidable churchman of the age. He refused to hand over a basilica to the Arian empress Justina in 386, defeated the senator Symmachus' plea to restore the Altar of Victory to the Senate house, and later forced Theodosius to do penance. His preaching drew [[augustine_of_hippo|Augustine]] to Christianity. In his career the Roman governing class is visible taking over the Church.

stops.title: One faith for the empire
stops.text: On 27 February 380, [[theodosius_i|Theodosius I]], a Spanish general made emperor after the disaster of Adrianople, issued the edict Cunctos populos from Thessalonica. All peoples under his rule were to follow the faith handed down by the apostle Peter to the Romans and now taught by bishops Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, the faith of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as equal Trinity. Those who disagreed were 'demented and insane' heretics, subject to divine and imperial punishment. For the first time a particular Christian doctrine was defined by law as the religion of the state. The Council of Constantinople in 381 confirmed it, and the Nicene Creed in the form still recited in churches today was largely fixed there.

stops.title: An emperor does penance
stops.text: In 390 a mob in Thessalonica lynched the Gothic commander Butheric, who had imprisoned a popular charioteer. Theodosius ordered reprisals, and soldiers massacred perhaps 7,000 people trapped in the circus. Ambrose wrote to the emperor privately, refusing to celebrate the Eucharist in his presence until he repented. After some months Theodosius appeared in the cathedral of Milan without his imperial insignia and did public penance. Later Christian writers turned the episode into a legend of the bishop barring the emperor from the church door. It was a dramatic statement of a new principle: that the emperor, too, was a son of the Church and subject to its moral judgement. In the East, emperors never accepted that principle in the same way.

stops.title: The fall of the Serapeum
stops.text: In 391 Theodosius issued laws forbidding sacrifice and closing temples. In Alexandria, the bishop Theophilus provoked riots by parading cult objects found in a temple, and pagans barricaded themselves in the Serapeum, the great temple of Sarapis on its hill, which housed a famous library annex. When imperial orders came, Christians and soldiers stormed it. A soldier struck the enormous statue of Sarapis with an axe; when no thunderbolt fell, the crowd tore it apart and burned it in the theatre. A church and a monastery were built on the site. For Christians the event was a triumph; for pagans like Eunapius, the end of an age. Only a single column, the so-called Pillar of Pompey of about 298, still stands there.

stops.title: The battle of the wind
stops.text: In 392 the Frankish general Arbogast set up a puppet emperor in the West, the rhetorician Eugenius, who was backed by pagan senators in Rome. Theodosius marched west in 394 and met them on the river Frigidus, the Vipava in modern Slovenia, under the Julian Alps. On the first day his Gothic allies, among them the young [[alaric_i|Alaric]], suffered heavy losses. On the second day a violent wind, the bora, blew dust into the faces of the western troops and turned back their missiles, according to Christian writers. The western army was routed; Eugenius was executed and Arbogast killed himself. Images of Jupiter had stood on the western side. Christian writers saw a judgement of God, and the old religion lost its last political champion.

stops.title: Chalcedon: the great divide
stops.text: Doctrine did not stop dividing. In 451 the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria convened the largest council of antiquity, with some 500 bishops, at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople. It defined Christ as one person 'in two natures', following the Tome of Pope Leo of Rome, and gave the bishop of Constantinople a rank second only to Rome, which Leo refused to accept. Much of Egypt and Syria rejected the formula and held to 'one nature' after the union, the miaphysite position. The division was never healed. It shaped the Coptic, Syriac and Armenian churches, it defined the politics of every emperor down to Heraclius, and it helped make Roman rule in Egypt and Syria fragile when the Persians and Arabs came.

tours.title: The end of the West
tours.summary: A century from Adrianople to the deposition of the last emperor in Italy: how the western empire lost its armies, its revenues and finally its reason to exist.

stops.title: Adrianople
stops.text: In 376 tens of thousands of Goths, fleeing the Huns, asked to be admitted across the Danube. The emperor [[valens|Valens]] agreed, hoping for recruits, but corrupt officials starved the refugees, selling them dog meat in exchange for their children as slaves. The Goths rose. On 9 August 378, outside Adrianople, Valens attacked their wagon laager without waiting for his nephew Gratian's western army, in the heat of the afternoon, with troops who had marched all morning. The Gothic cavalry returned from foraging and fell on the Roman flank. Ammianus says two thirds of the army died, with Valens himself, whose body was never found. It was the worst defeat since Cannae, and for the first time a whole people stayed inside the empire undefeated.

stops.title: Two empires
stops.text: Theodosius made peace with the Goths in 382, settling them as a people under their own leaders, obliged to fight for Rome. When he died in Milan on 17 January 395, he left the empire to his two sons, Arcadius, about 17, in Constantinople and [[honorius|Honorius]], ten, in the West. There had been divisions before, but this one was never reversed. The two courts became rivals, competing over Illyricum and its recruits, and each was run by a powerful minister: in the West the half-Vandal general [[stilicho|Stilicho]], married to Theodosius' niece Serena. The western half had the longer frontiers, the more exposed provinces, and a senatorial aristocracy that owned vast estates and paid little tax. Turn on the territory layer and watch the two halves diverge.

stops.title: The Rhine crossing
stops.text: On the last day of 406, according to Prosper's chronicle, Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz; the date may in fact be 405. The frontier troops had been stripped to defend Italy against Alaric and Radagaisus. The invaders spread through Gaul for three years, and Jerome, in Bethlehem, listed the cities destroyed. In Britain the army proclaimed its own emperor, Constantine III, who crossed to Gaul and was recognised by Honorius for a while. In 409 the invaders crossed the Pyrenees into Spain, where they divided the provinces by lot. Britain, cut off, expelled its Roman officials in 409 according to Zosimus, and in 410 Honorius reportedly told the British cities to see to their own defence. Roman rule there never returned.

stops.title: Rome sacked
stops.text: After Stilicho was executed in 408 and the families of his barbarian soldiers massacred, thousands of them joined [[alaric_i|Alaric]]. The Gothic king besieged Rome three times, demanding land and a command; Honorius, safe behind the marshes of Ravenna, refused. On 24 August 410, the Goths entered through the Salarian Gate. For three days they looted the city, though they spared those who took refuge in the basilicas of Peter and Paul. Galla Placidia, the emperor's sister, was taken hostage. It was the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in 800 years. Jerome wrote that 'the city that took the whole world was itself taken'. [[augustine_of_hippo|Augustine]] began the City of God to answer pagans who blamed the Christian god.

stops.title: Goths in Aquitaine
stops.text: After Alaric's death the Goths wandered through Italy, Gaul and Spain. In 418 the general Constantius settled them as federates in the valley of the Garonne, between Toulouse and Bordeaux, after they had destroyed the Siling Vandals and Alans in Spain on Rome's behalf. How they were provided for is fiercely debated. The older view is that Roman landowners gave up a third or two thirds of their estates; Walter Goffart argued that the Goths received shares of tax revenue instead. In either case a Gothic king now ruled a kingdom inside a Roman province. In the same year Honorius revived an annual council of the seven Gallic provinces at Arles. Within two generations the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse was an independent state reaching from the Loire deep into Spain.

stops.title: Carthage falls to the Vandals
stops.text: In 429 [[gaiseric|Gaiseric]] led the Vandals and Alans, perhaps 80,000 people, across the Strait of Gibraltar into Africa. They took Hippo in 431, a year after Augustine died during the siege. On 19 October 439, in peacetime, Gaiseric seized Carthage, the second city of the West. This was the most damaging blow of all. Africa was the West's richest region, supplying most of Rome's grain and perhaps half the taxes the western government still collected. Gaiseric built a fleet that raided Sicily and Italy, and the senators' African estates were confiscated. A joint eastern and western expedition to recover Carthage gathered in Sicily in 441 and was recalled when the Huns invaded the Balkans. From now on the western state was chronically short of money for its army.

stops.title: Attila in Gaul
stops.text: In 451 [[attila|Attila]] led the Huns and their subject peoples, Gepids, Ostrogoths and others, into Gaul. He sacked Metz and besieged Orléans. [[aetius|Aetius]], the general who had dominated the West for twenty years, assembled a coalition of Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians, Alans and what remained of the Roman army. In June they met on the Catalaunian Plains, somewhere near Troyes or Châlons. The Visigothic king Theodoric I was killed, but Attila was halted and withdrew. Jordanes' figure of 165,000 dead is fantasy, but the battle was a rare success. Note who won it, though: Roman generalship and diplomacy holding together barbarian kingdoms. In 452 Attila invaded Italy and destroyed Aquileia, and in 453 he died on his wedding night.

stops.title: The Vandals in Rome
stops.text: In 454 [[valentinian_iii|Valentinian III]] murdered Aetius with his own hands in the palace; a courtier told him he had cut off his right hand with his left. Six months later Aetius' retainers killed Valentinian on the Campus Martius, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West. The senator Petronius Maximus seized the throne and married Valentinian's widow, and Gaiseric, whose son had been betrothed to Valentinian's daughter, sailed for Rome. In June 455 the Vandals plundered the city for two weeks, methodically, carrying off the empress and her daughters, the gilded bronze roof tiles of the Capitoline temple, and, according to Procopius, the treasures of the Jerusalem Temple brought by Titus. Petronius was stoned by a mob as he fled.

stops.title: The great armada
stops.text: The last real chance to save the West came in 468. The eastern emperor Leo I and the western emperor Anthemius launched a combined expedition against the Vandals: Procopius says over a thousand ships and 100,000 men, at a cost of 64,000 pounds of gold and 700,000 of silver, more than a year's revenue of the eastern empire. The fleet under Basiliscus anchored near Cape Bon. Gaiseric asked for a five-day truce, waited for a favourable wind, and sent fireships into the crowded Roman fleet at night. Half the fleet burned. The expedition collapsed, the eastern treasury was emptied for a generation, and the Vandal kingdom survived until Belisarius. Without Africa, the western empire had no way to pay for an army of its own.

stops.title: The last emperor in Italy
stops.text: By the 470s the western emperor was a figure manipulated by his generals. In 475 the general Orestes, once Attila's secretary, made his young son Romulus emperor. The army in Italy, mostly barbarian federates, demanded a third of the land in Italy. Orestes refused. Their leader, [[odoacer|Odoacer]], a Scirian officer, killed Orestes at Placentia and in September 476 deposed Romulus, whom he pensioned off to a villa near Naples. Then he sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople, declaring through the Senate that one emperor was enough for both halves. He ruled Italy as king, kept the Senate and the Roman administration, and appointed consuls. Contemporaries barely noticed; the year 476 became an epoch only for later writers like Marcellinus Comes.

stops.title: The last legitimate emperor
stops.text: Romulus had never been recognised by Constantinople. The western emperor in eastern eyes was Julius Nepos, whom Orestes had driven out of Italy in 475 and who still ruled from Salona in Dalmatia. The eastern emperor [[zeno|Zeno]] told Odoacer's envoys to receive Nepos back; Odoacer issued coins in Nepos' name and ignored him. In 480 Nepos was murdered by his own retainers in his villa near Salona, possibly the palace of Diocletian. With him the line of western emperors ended. Odoacer annexed Dalmatia. Many historians argue that 480, not 476, is the end of the western empire in law, though no one at the time thought of either year as the end of Rome. The Senate in Rome continued to meet for another century.

stops.title: The last Roman in Gaul
stops.text: In northern Gaul a Roman enclave had survived, cut off from Italy, under the general Aegidius and his son Syagrius, whom Gregory of Tours calls 'king of the Romans', ruling from Soissons. In 486 the young Frankish king [[clovis_i|Clovis]] defeated Syagrius, who fled to the Visigoths and was handed back and killed. Within twenty years Clovis had converted to Catholic Christianity, beaten the Alamanni and driven the Visigoths out of most of Gaul at Vouillé in 507. The Franks, few in number, ruled through Gallo-Roman bishops and landowners, used Latin law and administration, and in 508 Clovis received the title of consul from the eastern emperor. End the tour here: the West did not fall in a day; it was replaced, kingdom by kingdom.

tours.title: Justinian's gamble
tours.summary: Law, war, plague and the dome of Hagia Sophia: the reign of an emperor who tried to restore the Roman empire of the Mediterranean, and what it cost.

stops.title: Making the law new
stops.text: [[justinian_i|Justinian]], nephew of a peasant soldier from the Balkans who had become emperor, succeeded his uncle Justin in 527. Within six months he appointed a commission to collect all valid imperial laws into a single code, issued in April 529. In 530 the quaestor Tribonian was ordered to do something even more ambitious: to read the works of the classical jurists, about 2,000 books and three million lines, and reduce them to a single coherent text. The Digest of 533, some 150,000 lines in fifty books, was completed in three years, with the Institutes, a textbook for students. A second edition of the Code followed in 534. Rediscovered in 11th-century Bologna, this body of Roman law became the foundation of the legal systems of continental Europe.

stops.title: Dara: a young general
stops.text: Justinian inherited a war with Persia. In June 530 a Persian army, said to number 40,000 or 50,000, advanced on the fortress city of Dara, built by Anastasius thirty years earlier right on the frontier near Nisibis. The Roman commander was [[belisarius|Belisarius]], about 25 years old. He dug a complex system of ditches in front of the city, with gaps through which his cavalry could charge, and posted Hunnic horsemen on the flanks. When the Persian Immortals broke through on the left, a hidden squadron of Heruls attacked them from behind a hill. The Persians were driven off with heavy losses. It was the first major Roman victory over Persia in generations. Procopius, the historian, was present as Belisarius' secretary.

stops.title: Nika
stops.text: In January 532 the Blue and Green circus factions, usually enemies, united in the hippodrome of Constantinople against the emperor's ministers, shouting 'Nika', 'conquer'. For five days they burned the city centre, including the church of Hagia Sophia and the Senate house, and proclaimed a nephew of Anastasius emperor. Justinian prepared to flee. Procopius gives [[theodora|Theodora]] a speech in the council: royalty is a good burial shroud. Belisarius and Mundus then led their soldiers into the hippodrome, where the crowd was packed together, and Narses bribed the Blues to leave. Procopius says some 30,000 people were killed. Justinian's power was never challenged in the capital again, and he began rebuilding at once on a scale nobody had seen.

stops.title: The dome of Hagia Sophia
stops.text: Forty days after the riots, work began on a new Hagia Sophia, designed by two men who were mathematicians and theorists of mechanics rather than builders, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. It was finished in under six years and dedicated on 27 December 537. Its dome, about 31 metres in diameter and 55 metres above the floor, seemed to Procopius to hang from heaven on a golden chain, because a ring of forty windows at its base dissolved its support in light. The building used pendentives on a scale never tried before. The first dome collapsed after an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt higher by Isidore's nephew. Justinian, according to a much later legend, said on entering: 'Solomon, I have surpassed you'.

stops.title: Africa recovered
stops.text: Using a dynastic coup among the Vandals as a pretext, Justinian sent Belisarius against Africa in 533 with only about 15,000 soldiers, against the advice of his ministers, who remembered 468. The fleet landed unopposed. Ten miles from Carthage, at Ad Decimum, on 13 September, the Vandal king Gelimer tried to trap the Romans with three converging columns; the attack was badly coordinated, his brother was killed, and Gelimer wasted time burying him. Belisarius entered Carthage two days later and ate the dinner prepared for Gelimer in the palace. After a second victory at Tricamarum, Gelimer surrendered in 534 and was led in a triumph in Constantinople. He is said to have repeated 'vanity of vanities' as he walked. A century-old kingdom had fallen in months.

stops.title: The year without summer
stops.text: In 536 Procopius, in Italy, wrote that 'the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during this whole year'. John Lydus in Constantinople and writers in Syria, Ireland and China describe the same dimming. Tree rings across the northern hemisphere show the coldest summers of the last two thousand years in 536 and the following decade, and ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica show sulphate from a large volcanic eruption early in 536, followed by another in 539-540. Crops failed from Ireland to China. Historians have proposed calling the period the Late Antique Little Ice Age. It is a reminder that Justinian's wars were fought in a climate crisis, and that the plague that followed found a weakened population.

stops.title: Belisarius in Rome
stops.text: In 535 Justinian turned on the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy. Belisarius took Sicily and Naples and in December 536 entered Rome with about 5,000 men. In February 537 the Gothic king Witiges arrived with a much larger army and besieged the city for a year and nine days. The Goths cut the aqueducts, which never ran fully again, and Belisarius set up floating mills on the Tiber to grind grain. The defenders threw statues from Hadrian's mausoleum onto the attackers. Witiges withdrew in March 538. By 540 Belisarius had taken Ravenna through a bluff, letting the Goths believe he would accept their offer to make him western emperor. Italy seemed won. It was to suffer fifteen more years of war.

stops.title: Antioch burns
stops.text: While the best Roman troops were in Italy, [[khosrow_i|Khosrow I]] broke the 'Eternal Peace' of 532 and invaded Syria in 540. He took Beroea, then Antioch, the third city of the empire, where he burned everything except the cathedral, and deported its population to a new city near Ctesiphon, which he named 'Khosrow's Better Antioch', with its own baths and hippodrome. On the way home he bathed in the Mediterranean at Seleucia and watched chariot races at Apamea, insisting that the Greens win because Justinian favoured the Blues. Other cities bought him off with gold. The war that followed, partly fought in the Caucasus over Lazica, lasted until 562, when a fifty-year peace was signed and Rome agreed to pay 30,000 solidi a year.

stops.title: The plague
stops.text: In 541 plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt and reached Constantinople in spring 542. Procopius, who saw it, describes buboes in the groin and armpit, delirium and death within days; at its height 10,000 people died each day in the capital, and towers of the city walls were filled with bodies. Ancient DNA from graves in Bavaria and elsewhere has confirmed that it was Yersinia pestis, bubonic plague, the first known pandemic of the disease. Justinian himself caught it and recovered. How many died across the empire is fiercely debated: older estimates of a quarter to half the population have been challenged as exaggerated. It returned roughly every fifteen years until the 8th century. Justinian kept fighting on every front.

stops.title: Taginae: the end of the Goths
stops.text: In 541 the Goths chose a brilliant new king, [[totila|Totila]], who recovered almost all of Italy, took Rome twice and freed slaves and tenants to fight for him. Justinian finally gave his eunuch chamberlain [[narses|Narses]], in his seventies, the money for a real army: about 30,000 men, many of them Lombards, Heruls and Gepids. At Busta Gallorum in the Apennines, in summer 552, Narses dismounted his barbarian cavalry in the centre and placed 8,000 archers on the wings in crescent formation. The Gothic cavalry charge was shot to pieces. Totila was killed in flight. A last Gothic army was destroyed at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius. Italy had been reconquered after eighteen years of war, but it was devastated, and Rome had perhaps 30,000 inhabitants.

stops.title: The verdict
stops.text: Justinian died in November 565, aged about 83. His empire stretched from southern Spain to the Euphrates, with the Mediterranean once more a Roman lake. Three years later the Lombards, who had fought for Narses at Taginae, crossed the Julian Alps under King Alboin with their families and Saxon allies. Within a few years they held most of northern Italy and duchies at Spoleto and Benevento, leaving the empire Ravenna, Rome, Naples and the far south. Slavs and Avars were crossing the Danube; the Visigoths would retake the Spanish province by 624. Was Justinian's reconquest a tragic overreach that left the empire exhausted, or the last time that the Roman Mediterranean was a reality? Historians still disagree. Continue with 'The last war of antiquity'.

tours.title: The last war of antiquity (602-641)
tours.summary: The great Roman-Persian war of 602-628, the most destructive in the history of the two empires, and the Arab conquests that followed it within a decade.

stops.title: The murder of Maurice
stops.text: [[maurice|Maurice]] was a capable emperor who had restored the Danube frontier and ended a Persian war on favourable terms in 591 by helping the young [[khosrow_ii|Khosrow II]] regain his throne. But he was short of money. In 602 he ordered the Danube army to winter north of the river, living off the Slavic lands. The soldiers mutinied, raised a junior officer named [[phocas|Phocas]] on a shield and marched on Constantinople. Maurice fled across the Bosporus and was caught at Chalcedon. Phocas had his five younger sons killed in front of him before he was beheaded on 27 November 602. Khosrow, who called Maurice his father, declared war to avenge him, with a young man presented as Maurice's surviving son Theodosius in his train.

stops.title: Heraclius sails from Carthage
stops.text: Phocas' reign was a disaster. The Persians took Dara in 604 and advanced into Asia Minor while Phocas purged the elite. In 608 the exarch of Africa, Heraclius the Elder, revolted. His son [[heraclius|Heraclius]] sailed for Constantinople with a fleet, its masts displaying icons of the Virgin, while his cousin Nicetas marched overland to take Egypt. On 5 October 610 Heraclius entered the capital, where the populace had already turned against Phocas. The tyrant was brought before him. 'Is this how you have governed the empire?' Heraclius asked. 'Will you govern it better?' Phocas replied. He was beheaded and his body mutilated. Heraclius was crowned the same day and married his betrothed, Fabia-Eudocia. The empire he inherited was close to collapse.

stops.title: Jerusalem falls
stops.text: The Persian general Shahrbaraz beat Heraclius outside Antioch in 613, cutting the empire in two, and took Damascus. In May 614 he took Jerusalem after a siege of about three weeks. The monk Strategius, who was taken captive, describes the slaughter of thousands, whose bodies were counted in the city's cisterns and churches, and the deportation of the patriarch Zacharias and many others to Persia. The relic of the True Cross was carried off to Ctesiphon. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was burned. The shock was enormous: the Holy City was lost to a Zoroastrian king. For the first time the war took on the character of a religious struggle, and Heraclius would later present his campaigns as a holy war.

stops.title: Egypt lost
stops.text: In 618-619 Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt, the empire's richest province and the source of the grain that fed Constantinople. Alexandria fell in 619, according to one account betrayed through a canal gate by a foreign student. Persian rule in Egypt lasted ten years, and papyri show the Persians governing efficiently through the existing Roman officials. In Constantinople the free bread distribution, which had existed since Constantine, ended in 618. Meanwhile the Avars raided to the walls of the capital, and the Slavs settled across the Balkans. Heraclius is said to have considered moving the capital to Carthage, until the patriarch made him swear in the church of Hagia Sophia not to abandon the city. By 620 the empire had lost almost everything east of Asia Minor.

stops.title: The emperor takes the field
stops.text: No emperor had led an army in person since Theodosius I. On 5 April 622, after Easter, Heraclius left Constantinople to train his army in Asia Minor, taking with him an icon of Christ not made by human hands. To pay for the war, the patriarch Sergius had lent him the gold and silver plate of the churches, which was melted down into coin, and soldiers' pay was halved. Heraclius spent the summer drilling the troops in mock battles, then outmanoeuvred Shahrbaraz in Cappadocia and won a victory. George of Pisidia, a deacon of Hagia Sophia, wrote poems on the campaign that survive. The poems present it as a crusade, with Heraclius as a new David. The tide had begun to turn.

stops.title: Into Persia
stops.text: In 624 Heraclius did what no Roman general had done before: instead of defending the provinces, he struck through Armenia into the heart of the Persian empire. He took Ganzak in Atropatene and destroyed the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp at Takht-e Soleyman, one of the three holiest fires of Zoroastrianism, where Sasanian kings walked on foot from Ctesiphon after their coronation. It was revenge for Jerusalem. Heraclius then wintered in the Caucasus, recruiting Lazi, Abasgi and Iberians, and fought a war of movement against three Persian armies sent to trap him, beating each in turn. For two years he lived off the enemy's land, cut off from his capital, while the Persians prepared a decisive blow against Constantinople itself.

stops.title: The siege of 626
stops.text: In summer 626 an Avar khagan with perhaps 80,000 Avars, Slavs and Bulgars attacked the land walls of Constantinople, while a Persian army under Shahrbaraz waited across the Bosporus at Chalcedon. Heraclius, in Lazica, did not return; he sent part of his army back and left the city to the patrician Bonus and the patriarch Sergius, who carried icons of the Virgin along the walls. The Avars attacked with siege towers for ten days. The key was the sea: the Slavs tried to ferry Persian troops across in their dugout canoes, and the Roman fleet destroyed them in the Golden Horn. The khagan burned his engines and withdrew. The city credited the Virgin; the Akathist hymn has long been associated with the deliverance.

stops.title: Nineveh
stops.text: In 627 Heraclius, now allied with the Western Turks, who besieged Tbilisi with him, marched south into Mesopotamia in autumn, an unusual season for campaigning. On 12 December, near the ruins of Nineveh on the Tigris, he met the Persian general Rhahzadh in a battle that lasted all day in fog. Heraclius killed Rhahzadh in single combat, according to the sources, and the Persian army was destroyed. The emperor advanced towards Ctesiphon, sacking Khosrow's palace at Dastagird, where he found 300 Roman standards captured in earlier wars. Khosrow II fled. The war that had brought Persia to the Bosporus and the Nile was won in a single campaign that had taken the war to the enemy's heartland.

stops.title: The fall of the King of Kings
stops.text: In February 628 Khosrow II was overthrown by his son Kavad II Shiroe and the Persian nobility, imprisoned in the 'house of darkness' and killed, it was said, after watching his sons executed. Kavad made peace at once, restoring the frontiers of 602 and promising to return the True Cross. But the Sasanian empire then dissolved into civil war: between 628 and 632 more than ten kings and queens ruled, including the two daughters of Khosrow, Boran and Azarmidokht. Shahrbaraz, the conqueror of Jerusalem and Egypt, seized the throne with Roman support in 630 and was murdered within weeks. Heraclius took the title basileus, the Greek word for king, which became the standard title of emperors from now on.

stops.title: The Cross returns to Jerusalem
stops.text: On 21 March 630, according to the date most historians now accept, Heraclius entered Jerusalem with his wife Martina, carrying the relic of the True Cross, which Shahrbaraz had handed back. He showed the patriarch Modestus that the seals on its reliquary were unbroken. It was the emotional climax of the reign and, in a sense, of late antiquity: a Christian Roman emperor, victorious over the ancient enemy, restoring the holiest relic of Christendom to the Holy City. The Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross later absorbed the memory. Heraclius also ordered the forced baptism of Jews, whom he blamed for collaborating with the Persians. Within eight years Jerusalem would surrender to the Caliph Umar.

stops.title: The Yarmuk
stops.text: Arab raiders from the new Muslim state united by Muhammad had appeared on the Palestinian frontier from 629. In 634 they beat a Roman army at Ajnadayn and took Damascus in 635. Heraclius gathered a large army, perhaps 15,000 to 40,000 men, Armenians, Christian Arabs of the Ghassanid confederation and regular troops, and sent it against them. In August 636, on the Yarmuk river, on the plateau above its gorge, the Roman army was defeated over six days of fighting; the decisive moment came when the Arab cavalry cut off the Roman retreat and many were driven into the ravines. Heraclius left Syria, saying, according to an Arabic tradition, 'Farewell, Syria, my fair province, this is the last goodbye'. Syria and Palestine were lost for good.

stops.title: The end of antiquity
stops.text: Heraclius died on 11 February 641, ill, perhaps with dropsy, and blamed by many for his marriage to his niece Martina. Mesopotamia, Syria and Palestine were gone; Egypt, invaded in 639, was signing away Alexandria by treaty that November. In the twenty-five years after 602 the empire had lost and recovered the whole East, then lost most of it again. Persia, the great rival of four centuries, would fall to the Arabs by 651. The Roman empire survived, centred on Constantinople, Asia Minor and the Aegean, Greek-speaking and Orthodox, the state modern historians call Byzantine. Here, in 641, this atlas ends. Its people, of course, still called themselves Romans, and would for another eight hundred years.
